citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The licensee and facility representative had not provided adequate veterinary care for a cavy seen during inspection and
did not communicate with the attending veterinarian in a timely manner.
Inspectors observed an adult male Patagonian cavy with an eye condition causing severe discomfort. The representative
said that he was aware that the cavy had been injured on or around four days before the inspection, but had not spoken
with the Attending Veterinarian (AV).
The cavy was unkempt, it walked with an unstable gait, and it was seen repeatedly pawing at its left eye and shaking its
head. An area of swelling and redness around the third eyelid (by the nose) was seen, the eyelids were drooping, and
there was noticeable discharge around the bottom of the eye. Many flies appeared to be attracted to the injury (flies were
not bothering the healthy cavy in this manner) and were causing it additional discomfort. The animal frequently stopped
walking and lay down.
Because the facility representatives had not contacted the AV about this cavy's condition prior to inspection, at the
inspectors' request, he contacted the AV during the inspection to seek appropriate care.
Failure to contact the AV in a timely manner while having sick or injured animals without obtaining consultation or
treatment does not provide for their health or wellbeing.
***The AV had the representative provide adequate care on the afternoon of 10/6/2026. Inspectors stopped the inspection
early so that the cavy’s care could be addressed.
***Corrected at time of inspection.

At the time of inspection, the inventory, acquisition and disposition records were incomplete. Some of the animals did not
have birth dates recorded nor information regarding animal dispositions, including:
-Disposition records for an alpaca and 2 cavies sold were incomplete and unable to be obtained.
-The inventory for the Black Hawaiian sheep showed 12 animals but only 9 were counted during the inspection.
Records for the acquisition and disposition of animals are necessary to be able to accurately track animals being used in
regulated activities to ensure their legal acquisition, disposition details, proper care and humane transportation. The
exhibitor shall make, keep, and maintain records or forms which fully and correctly disclose information concerning
animals purchased or otherwise acquired, owned, held, leased, or otherwise in his possession or under his control, or
which is transported, sold, euthanized, or otherwise disposed of. The records shall include any offspring born of any
animal while in their possession or under their control. All information found within section 2.75 (b)(1) shall be recorded,
maintained, and made available for inspection.
***Correct by October 30th, 2026.

At the time of the inspection, the licensee did not have a written contingency plan in place. A written
emergency/contingency plan is required to ensure animal health and well-being in the event of an emergency or disaster.
Without a proper plan animals could suffer illness, injury or death due to unpreparedness during an emergency or
disaster. The licensee must develop, document and follow an appropriate plan to provide for the humane handling,
treatment, transportation, housing and care of their animals in the event of an emergency or disaster.

citations.desc: Environment enhancement to promote psychological well-being.
citations.narrative:
At the time of inspection, the environmental enhancement/enrichment plan for non-human primates (lemurs) had been
started but had not been reviewed and approved by the attending veterinarian (AV). Lack of an AV-approved
environmental enrichment plan for the lemurs does not ensure their environmental and social needs are adequately
provided. The plan must be developed to address all the requirements of section 3.81 and approved by the attending
veterinarian.

APHIS officials observed rat-sized active rodent holes very close to the lemur shelter and enclosure housing three ringtail
lemurs. The lemurs are fed pellets and produce directly on the concrete floor of the enclosure. Pests can transmit
disease, contaminate feed and surfaces, and can harm animals. Food and food receptacles, if used, must be located to
minimize any risk of contamination by excreta and pests.
***Correct by October 30th, 2026.

A black Hawaiian spring lamb was noted to have gotten its head caught under the fence and died on 8/1/2026 according
to facility records. Failure to maintain facilities in a manner that protects the animals from injury doesn’t meet the AWA
requirements. Ensure that the area where it got stuck is repaired to prevent further recurrence.
During the inspection, two goat kids were observed sticking their heads under an approximately 5-inch tall gap under the
fence with their necks touching the bottom points of the chain-link fencing to eat grass outside the enclosure.
The cavy enclosure had mesh fencing that was coming away from the fence with sharp metal points that the animals can
contact.
The pasture housing the Barbado sheep had chicken wire in disrepair on the entry gate that had sharp metal points that
animals could contact. Additionally, the enclosure had an approximately 4 ft by 8 ft large fence panel and similarly sized
gate stacked together on the ground that the animals could step on, as well as a round-bale feeder with pieces of upward
turned sharp edges the animals could contact.
The enclosure next to the zebras housing one adult goat had loose metal and fence panel points sticking out that the goat
could touch.
Sharp points in animal enclosures can cause injury. Ensure that housing facilities are structurally sound and maintained in
good repair to protect the animals from injury.

Three kangaroos died within the same week (7/5/2026, 7/7/2026, and 7/10/2026). The Attending Veterinarian (AV)’s
findings of dead kangaroos (findings of external carcass; no necropsy done per the AV) suggest that two kangaroos likely
had eaten rat poison; they were pale and had signs of abnormal bleeding, per the AV. The licensee conveyed that he
places rat poison in rodent holes and covers them with dirt. The location of the kangaroos’ feeders in relation to the rodent
holes, coupled with rat poison placement, creates a risk of poisoning to animals. The licensee must ensure that the pest
control program against mammalian pests is safe and effective.
APHIS officials also observed rat-sized rodent holes very close to the enclosures, shelters, and feeding areas for the
kangaroo and muntjac deer. Pests can transmit disease, contaminate feed and surfaces, and can harm animals. A safe
and effective programs for the control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests shall be established and
maintained.
***Correct from this day forward October 8, 2026.

The facility does not appear to have enough employees to adequately perform thorough daily observations of the animals,
maintain enclosures and shelters in good repair, maintain an effective pest control program, relay information in a timely
manner to the attending veterinarian, and keep required records up to date. This can cause unnecessary animal
discomfort, delay veterinary care, and expose animals to hazardous conditions within their enclosures and surrounding
environment. There are only 2 part-time employees and the main facility representative caring for all the animals. When
asked why the veterinarian wasn’t contacted sooner regarding the cavy’s injuries, the representative conveyed that there
is too much to do. A sufficient number of adequately trained employees shall be utilized to maintain the professionally
acceptable level of husbandry practices set forth in this subpart. Such practices shall be under a supervisor who has a
background in animal care.
***Correct by October 30th, 2026.

The Moluccan cockatoos and macaw have a panel between their enclosures that has a wire point and screw points that
they could contact. Wire points and screw points can cause injury. Ensure that their enclosures are free from sharp points.
***Correct by 10/15/2026.

citations.desc: Environment enhancement to promote psychological well-being.
citations.narrative:
At the time of inspection, the written environmental enhancement/enrichment plan for birds had been signed but did not
include all species at the facility. Lack of an environmental enrichment plan covering all bird species does not ensure that
environmental and social needs are properly provided. The plan must be developed to address the social, environmental
and special considerations for all birds at the facility and approved by the AV.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
APHIS officials observed rat-sized active rodent holes very close to the enclosures, shelters, and feeding areas for the
ringneck pheasants, silver pheasant and guinea hen. During the inspection live rats were observed in the guinea hen and
pheasant enclosures. Pests can transmit disease, contaminate feed and surfaces, and can harm animals. A safe and
effective program for the control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests shall be established and
maintained to promote the health and well-being of the birds and reduce contamination by pests in animal areas.
***Correct by October 30th, 2026
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the licensee and facility representative.

any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
